::: {.lead}
The writers of *Night Owl Games* hand over the script of the opening of
*Rooftop Rescue*. By Thursday, the storyboard artist must turn it into a
board that the 3D team can build from. Where does one panel end and the next
begin? How much detail does a panel need? How does the artist know that the
board is ready? In lecture 9 you learned shots, composition and flow. In this
seminar you **draw** a storyboard from a scene, step by step: break the scene
into beats, draw quick panels, and check the board. Every section ends with
a short task, and at the end you have your own board.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary storyboard story-beat panel panel-caption thumbnail-sketch camera-move shot wide-shot close-up screen-direction >}}

## 10.1 Where does a panel start? From scene to beats

A script is a list of actions and lines. A storyboard is a list of shots. To
go from one to the other, the artist first marks the **beats** of the scene
(lecture 4): the small steps where something changes (@fig-beats).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.1 — One panel per beat"}
Mark a new beat when **something changes**: a new place, a new action, a new
speaker, or a new feeling. Each beat gets at least one **panel**. A long beat
can get two panels, for example a wide shot and then a close-up.
:::

![The script of the opening, its five beats, and one panel for each beat.](images/scene-beats.png){#fig-beats width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.1 — The beats of the opening"}
1. "EXT. FLOODED STREET – DUSK. Water fills the street." A new place:
   beat 1, a wide shot.
2. "Nour jumps into the boat." A new action: beat 2, a medium shot.
3. "NOUR: Hold on, everyone." A new speaker: beat 3, a close-up.
4. "She rows to the roof." A new action: beat 4, a medium shot.
5. "SALMA: I won't leave without my cat." A new speaker and a feeling:
   beat 5, a close-up.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.2 — Two lines, one beat"}
Salma says: "I won't leave without my cat. He's afraid of water." Both
sentences come from the same speaker with the same feeling: one beat, one
close-up, and the caption holds both sentences.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
One panel for every sentence of the script. A board of 40 panels for a
30-second scene is slow to draw and hard to read. Change panels when
something changes, not at every line.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/board-builder.html" poster="sims/board-builder.png" title="Board Builder: choose a shot for each beat and check the board" height="900" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Beats of a short scene"}
Here is a short scene of *Rooftop Rescue*: "INT. SALMA'S KITCHEN – NIGHT.
Water comes under the door. Salma lifts the cat onto the table. SALMA: Stay
here, Pasha. A light shines through the window. NOUR (V.O.): Salma? Are you
in there?"

1. Mark the beats. Write next to each one what changes.
2. In **Board Builder** (above), build the opening board and press "Check my
   board".

*Your result:* the scene with its beats marked, and a board without red
notes.
:::

## 10.2 Draw it fast: thumbnails, arrows and captions

The board artist does not draw a finished picture. A panel is a **thumbnail
sketch**: a small, fast drawing with simple shapes, made in one or two
minutes (@fig-panel).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.2 — The parts of a panel"}
A panel has: a **number**; a **frame** with the shape of the screen (16:9
for most games); simple shapes for the place and the characters; **arrows**
for movement in the shot; a dashed box and an arrow for a **camera move**
(a zoom or a pan); and under it a **caption** with the shot size, the action,
the dialogue or sound, and the time in seconds.
:::

![A panel drawn in two minutes, with its parts.](images/panel-anatomy.png){#fig-panel width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.3 — Drawing panel 2"}
1. Draw the frame, and a line for the water two thirds down.
2. Draw the boat as a long shape and Nour as a circle and a body, on the
   left third.
3. Draw an arrow to the right: she rows towards the roof.
4. Caption: "2 · Medium. Nour jumps into the boat and rows. SFX: splash,
   oars. 3 s."
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.4 — A camera move"}
The board wants the camera to come closer to Salma while she speaks. The
artist draws the wide shot of the roof, a dashed box around Salma's face (the
end of the move) and an arrow from a corner of the frame to the box. Caption:
"5 · Wide to close-up (zoom in). SALMA: I won't leave without my cat. 3 s."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A panel without a caption. The 3D team cannot guess the sound, the line or
the time from the drawing alone. Every panel needs its number and caption.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Draw five panels"}
On a storyboard sheet (or an A4 paper with five 16:9 boxes), draw the five
beats of Example 10.1.

1. Use simple shapes; take about two minutes per panel.
2. Add the arrows and a caption with shot size, action or line, sound and
   time.

*Your result:* five numbered panels with captions.
:::

## 10.3 Is the board ready? Check and time it

Before the team builds the scene, the artist checks the board with a short
list, and adds up the time of the panels (@fig-check).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.3 — The board checklist"}
A board is ready when: every beat has a panel; panel 1 shows the place; the
shot sizes change with the purpose; feelings are close-ups; the screen
direction stays the same; and every panel has a caption and a time. The sum
of the times is the length of the scene.
:::

![The checklist and the time line of a board.](images/board-check.png){#fig-check width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.5 — Timing the opening"}
The five panels have 3 s, 3 s, 2 s, 4 s and 3 s.

1. 3 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 3 = 15 seconds.
2. The producer wants the opening under 20 seconds, so the board fits.
3. Panel 4 (4 s of rowing) is the longest: if time is short, it is the first
   to cut.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.6 — A board that is not ready"}
A draft board has: panel 1 a close-up of Nour; panel 2 Nour rows right to
left; panel 3 Salma's line in a wide shot of the roof.

1. No establishing shot: add a wide shot of the street first.
2. Check the direction of panel 2 against the rest of the board.
3. Salma's fear is too far away: change panel 3 to a close-up.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Checking only the drawings. A board can look good and still break a rule:
read it with the checklist, one line at a time.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Check your own board"}
Use your five panels of section 10.2.

1. Go through the six points of the checklist. Mark each one yes or no, and
   fix every no.
2. Add up the times. Is the scene under 20 seconds?

*Your result:* the checked board and its total time.
:::

## Case study: the board review at Night Owl Games

Every Thursday, the team of *Night Owl Games* reviews the storyboards of
*Rooftop Rescue* before the 3D artists start. Five boards of the opening lie
on the table. One starts with a close-up of Nour; one has Nour rowing left to
right and then right to left; one shows Nour twice in the same medium shot;
one shows Salma's fearful line in a wide shot of the roof; and one starts
wide, then shows the action in a medium shot and Salma's line in a close-up.
The team must find what is wrong with each board. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses these boards. In the mini-game below you review
them.

{{< sim file="sims/board-fixer.html" poster="sims/board-fixer.png" title="Board Fixer: find the problem in each storyboard" kind="game" height="560" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapters on story and on
indirect control. Search the web for "storyboard template 16:9" to print a
free sheet.

## Exercises

1. When does a scene get a new beat? Give four kinds of change.
2. Salma says two sentences with the same feeling. How many panels?
3. Why is "one panel per sentence" a bad rule?
4. What is a thumbnail sketch?
5. Name five parts of a panel.
6. How do you draw a zoom in a panel?
7. What must every caption have?
8. Five panels have 2 s, 3 s, 3 s, 4 s and 2 s. How long is the scene?
9. A board starts with a close-up of a face. Which point of the checklist
   does it break?
10. *Night Owl Games*: a board shows Salma's fearful line in a wide shot.
    What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. When something changes: a new place, a new action, a new speaker or a new feeling.
2. One panel (one close-up) with both sentences in the caption.
3. The board gets too long, slow to draw and hard to read.
4. A small, fast drawing of a panel with simple shapes.
5. The number, the 16:9 frame, simple shapes, movement arrows, camera-move arrows, the caption.
6. A dashed box for the end of the move and an arrow to it.
7. The shot size, the action or the line, the sound and the time.
8. 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 14 seconds.
9. Panel 1 must show the place (an establishing wide shot).
10. Her fear is too far away to see; use a close-up of Salma.
:::
